arabic_grammar_name: tamyiz asnaf al-harf al-akhir fi al-ism (discriminating final-letter noun classes) qabla tatbiq qa'idat al-i'rab al-mahjub
plain_rule: A noun or participle's case-marking (i'rab) behavior is decided by which FINAL-LETTER CLASS it belongs to, and that class must be certified before any 'hidden exponent' rule is applied -- the classes are not interchangeable and do not share one declension: a weak-final (manqus) noun/participle whose bare final radical is a single glide preceded by kasra (qadin/da'in) drops that glide in the INDEFINITE nominative and genitive, replacing it with tanwin kasratan alone, and keeps it only in the indefinite accusative and throughout the definite forms; an otherwise similar noun whose final glide is instead GEMINATED (doubled under a shadda, so two radicals merge rather than one bare radical standing alone) does not qualify for that class at all and declines as an ordinary sound-final noun, with a visible vowel and tanwin on the geminated letter in all three cases; an alif-final (maqsura) noun cannot carry any vowel on its final alif in any case, so its case stays covert (muqaddar) in all three slots and its written nunation is one single invariant shape, never varying by case; and a noun ending in a hamza after a long vowel is a full consonant-final noun whose hamza bears its own case vowel and tanwin directly and visibly, so the manqus noun's hidden-exponent rule must never be extended to it.
trigger_condition: a noun, adjective, or participle ending in a weak glide, a geminated glide, a long alif, or a hamza is being declined for case, and the final-letter class has not been certified (gemination checked, glide-vs-alif-vs-hamza distinguished) before a hidden-exponent or full-declension rule is applied
expected_feature: the final-letter class certified first (single bare glide after kasra vs. geminated glide vs. alif vs. post-long-vowel hamza), then the case/nunation behavior specific to that class applied: dropped glide + bare tanwin kasratan for indefinite nominative/genitive manqus forms, full visible declension for a geminated-final noun, one invariant covert-case nunation shape for an alif-final noun, and a directly-marked visible case vowel/tanwin on a hamza-final noun
typical_error_feature: a noun classified as weak-final (manqus) merely because a glide sits at the end, without checking for gemination first; the weak glide kept visible with a vowel in the indefinite nominative or genitive instead of dropped; a visible short vowel written on an alif-final noun's own alif, or its nunation shape varied by case; or the manqus hidden-exponent rule extended to a hamza-final noun whose hamza actually bears its exponent directly
point_template: Before you decline this noun's final letter, certify its class -- is the final letter a single bare glide, a geminated glide, an alif, or a post-long-vowel hamza? -- because each class marks case differently.
teach_template: A weak-final (manqus) noun drops its single bare final glide (preceded by kasra) in the indefinite nominative and genitive, replacing it with tanwin kasratan, but keeps it in the indefinite accusative and throughout the definite forms; a geminated-final noun does not qualify for that class and declines as an ordinary sound noun; an alif-final (maqsura) noun never takes a visible vowel on its alif and uses one invariant nunation shape across all three cases; and a hamza-final noun after a long vowel marks its case directly and visibly on the hamza, never hiding it the way a manqus noun does.
bottom_out_template: Name the noun's certified final-letter class (bare glide / geminated glide / alif / hamza) and state exactly how that class marks (or covers, or hides) its case in this slot.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner extends a weak-final noun's hidden-case-exponent rule to a hamza-final noun, whose hamza actually marks its case directly and visibly.
A learner classifies a noun with a geminated final glide as weak-final (manqus) without first checking that the glide is doubled, not a single bare radical.

arabic_grammar_name: sighat al-mabni lil-majhul (passive-voice template, na'ib al-fa'il case, and agent omission)
plain_rule: Arabic passive voice (al-mabni lil-majhul) is signalled entirely by a FIXED VOWEL PAIRING on the stem (damma-kasra in the perfect, damma-fatha in the imperfect), never by any added or substituted consonant, so any other vowel combination fails to encode the passive regardless of which consonants are present; for a middle-weak (hollow) root the sound-stem passive template cannot be applied letter-by-consonant, because the hollow root's medial radical is a glide that cannot itself carry a vowel the way an ordinary consonant does -- the root class must be checked first, and the hollow-root passive instead realizes as a single long vowel across the whole stem. When a verb is put into the passive, its original direct object is promoted to fill the subject slot (na'ib al-fa'il) and takes NOMINATIVE case from that new syntactic position, not the accusative case it carried as an object before promotion. And because the na'ib al-fa'il construction is defined by the agent's absence, no agent-naming phrase (modelled on an English by-phrase or otherwise) may be attached to it; if the agent genuinely must be named, the fix is to switch to an active clause instead, never to bolt an agent phrase onto the passive.
trigger_condition: a verb is being put into the passive voice, or a promoted noun's case or the presence of a named agent in a passive sentence is being decided, and the vowel-pairing template, the root class (sound vs. hollow), the promoted noun's new syntactic position, or the agent-absence requirement has not been checked
expected_feature: the passive realized by its fixed vowel pairing (never a substituted consonant), the root's class (sound vs. hollow) checked before selecting which passive template applies, the promoted noun (na'ib al-fa'il) marked nominative from its new position rather than left in its pre-promotion accusative, and no agent-naming phrase attached to the passive construction
typical_error_feature: a vowel combination other than the fixed damma-kasra/damma-fatha pairing used for the passive; the sound-stem passive template applied consonant-by-consonant to a hollow root's medial radical; a promoted noun left in the accusative case it held as an object before promotion; or an agent-naming phrase (modelled on an English by-phrase) attached to a construction defined by agent absence
point_template: Before you form or read this passive, name the exact vowel pairing, check the root's class if it is weak, and check the case of any promoted noun and the presence of any agent phrase.
teach_template: The passive is carried by one fixed vowel pairing per tense, never by a consonant change; a hollow root's medial radical cannot bear that vowel directly and instead yields a long-vowel passive melody; the promoted object takes nominative case from its new subject position, not the accusative it had before; and the na'ib al-fa'il construction is defined by omitting the agent, so naming one there is never correct -- an active clause is used instead when the agent must be named.
bottom_out_template: Name the passive's exact vowel pairing (or its hollow-root realization), the case of the promoted noun from its new position, and whether any agent phrase is licensed here.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner applies the sound-stem passive template letter-by-consonant to a hollow root's medial radical instead of selecting the hollow-root passive melody.
A learner leaves the promoted noun (na'ib al-fa'il) in the accusative case it carried as an object before the verb was made passive.

arabic_grammar_name: tamyiz harf al-qalab min harf al-jadhr fi al-mushtaqqat al-ismiyya (excluding a nominal template's own consonant from the root, and reading a participle template by its prefix/vowel skeleton)
plain_rule: A nominal derivative template's own fixed consonant (such as the initial mim of an instrument-noun or an augmented-form active/passive-participle prefix) is never a root letter merely because it sits adjacent to the root -- it is excluded from the root by matching the whole surface against the closed template inventory, leaving the genuine triliteral root once the template's own consonant is stripped off. Separately, when two nominal derivatives share the same root consonants (an agent template such as fa'il and a patient template such as maf'ul), the two are told apart by their own prefix and internal vowel skeleton, not by their shared radicals -- reading the shared radicals while ignoring which of the two templates is actually present reverses who acted and what was acted upon.
trigger_condition: a nominal derivative's core/root letters are being identified, or two derivatives sharing one root but different agent/patient templates are being read or translated, and the template inventory has not been checked before a letter is counted as a root letter or a template is assumed from the shared radicals alone
expected_feature: a template's own fixed consonant excluded from the root by checking it against the closed template inventory, and an agent-template vs. patient-template reading decided by the derivative's own prefix and vowel skeleton rather than by the radicals the two forms share
typical_error_feature: a nominal-derivative template's own consonant (an instrument-noun mim, an augmented-form participle prefix) counted as a root letter, producing a root that does not exist; or an agent participle and a patient participle of one root swapped in translation because their shared radicals were read while the templates' own prefix/vowel skeleton was ignored
point_template: Before you name this word's root, check whether a nominal template owns one of its consonants -- and before you translate it, read the prefix and vowel skeleton, not just the radicals it shares with a related form.
teach_template: A nominal derivative template's own fixed consonant is excluded from the root by matching against the closed template inventory, never counted merely from adjacency; and two derivatives of one root built on different templates (agent vs. patient) are distinguished by their own prefix and vowel skeleton, since the shared radicals alone assign no argument role.
bottom_out_template: Name which letters belong to the template versus the root, and name the exact prefix/vowel skeleton that identifies which of the two derivative templates is present.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner counts a nominal derivative template's own initial consonant among the root letters, producing a root that does not exist in the dictionary.
A learner translates an agent-template participle as if it were the patient-template participle of the same root, reversing who acted and what was acted upon.

arabic_grammar_name: istiqlal i'rab al-mudaf ilayhi fi al-idafa, wa dabt hujaj al-masdar al-'amil (idafa second-term genitive independence, and a governing masdar's argument case)
plain_rule: In a construct (idafa), the second term is genitive by virtue of the construct relation ITSELF, independently of whatever case the first (head) term carries from its own governor -- the head's case never propagates to the second term. This independence is what licenses a governing verbal noun's (masdar's) own two arguments: its logical AGENT surfaces as the second term of an idafa built on the masdar and so is genitive, never nominative (nominative would wrongly treat it as if it were a verb's own subject); its logical OBJECT, by contrast, is governed the way the parent verb would govern it -- accusative -- and is not folded into the idafa chain as if it were a second genitive term. Separately, a verbal noun's own template is derived from the verb's own measure and realizes any weak radical the template's own slots require, never by copying the finite verb's own surface alteration (a weak radical that the verb's own perfect template collapses into a long vowel can sit as a plain, unaltered vowelless consonant in the masdar's own different template slot).
trigger_condition: a construct's second term's case is being decided, or a verbal noun's agent or object is being cased, or a verbal noun's own template is being derived from a verb whose surface shows a weak-radical alteration, and the idafa-independence rule, the agent/object case split, or the masdar's own template slots have not been checked
expected_feature: a construct's second term marked genitive regardless of the first term's own case, a governing masdar's agent marked genitive as the idafa's second term, its object marked accusative as the parent verb would govern it (not folded into the idafa chain), and a masdar's weak radical realized in the masdar template's own slot rather than copied from the finite verb's own altered surface
typical_error_feature: a construct's second term given the same case as the first term instead of genitive; a governing masdar's agent marked nominative as if it were a verb's subject; a governing masdar's object marked genitive as a further idafa term instead of accusative; or a masdar's weak radical altered to match the finite verb's own collapsed surface instead of realized in the masdar template's own stable slot
point_template: Before you case this construct's second term or this masdar's arguments, name the construct-genitive rule, and check whether the slot is the masdar's agent (genitive, second idafa term) or its object (accusative, parent-verb government) -- and derive the masdar's own weak-radical slot from its own template, not from the verb's surface.
teach_template: A construct's second term is genitive from the construct relation itself, never from the first term's own case; a governing verbal noun's agent is genitive as the idafa's second term while its object stays accusative under parent-verb government, never folded into the idafa chain; and a verbal noun's weak radical is realized in the masdar template's own slot, never copied unchanged from the finite verb's own altered surface.
bottom_out_template: Name the construct-genitive rule, classify the slot as agent (genitive) or object (accusative), and name the masdar template's own weak-radical realization.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner lets the case of a construct's first term propagate onto its second term instead of marking the second term genitive from the construct relation itself.
A learner assumes a verbal noun's weak radical must show the same alteration as the finite verb's own perfect-tense surface, instead of deriving it from the masdar template's own slot.

arabic_grammar_name: shurut isti'mal ism al-fa'il (huwiyya/hala) muqabil al-hadath al-mahdud, wa tamyiz al-hal 'an al-na't al-mu'arraf (licensing conditions for a participle's identity/state reading against a single bounded event, and telling a circumstantial apart from a definite attribute)
plain_rule: An active participle names an identity, role, or persisting state of its referent, never a single bounded past occurrence -- describing a one-time completed event requires the perfect (finite) verb instead, and the derivational form actually used must be selected from the event actually intended, not from whichever form is simpler or comes to mind first. Separately, a participle-shaped modifier that AGREES with its head noun in definiteness and case is an ordinary attribute (na't), which copies its head's definiteness and case, and is not a circumstantial (hal); a hal is always indefinite and accusative regardless of its head's own case or definiteness, because it describes the head's state at the time of the main verb rather than agreeing with the head as a modifier does -- the definiteness-agreement test must be run before either label is assigned.
trigger_condition: a participle is being chosen to express a past event, or a participle-shaped modifier's role (attribute vs. circumstantial) is being decided, and the identity/state-vs-event distinction or the definiteness-agreement test has not been checked first
expected_feature: a participle used only for an identity, role, or persisting state (never a bounded single past event, which takes the perfect verb instead), the derivational form chosen from the event actually intended, and a participle-shaped modifier classified as attribute (agrees in definiteness and case with its head) or circumstantial (always indefinite and accusative regardless of its head) only after the definiteness-agreement test
typical_error_feature: a participle used to narrate a specific, bounded past event instead of the perfect verb; a derivational form chosen because it is simpler or more available rather than because it matches the intended event; or a definite, case-agreeing modifier labelled a circumstantial (hal) without running the definiteness-agreement test, or an indefinite accusative hal treated as if it needed to agree with its head
point_template: Before you use this participle, ask whether you mean an identity/state or a single bounded event -- and before you label this modifier, run the definiteness-agreement test against its head.
teach_template: A participle names an identity, role, or persisting state, never a single bounded past occurrence (which needs the perfect verb), and the derivational form used must match the event actually intended rather than whichever is simplest; a participle-shaped modifier that agrees with its head in definiteness and case is an ordinary attribute, while a circumstantial is always indefinite and accusative regardless of its head, so the definiteness-agreement test decides the label.
bottom_out_template: State whether an identity/state or a bounded event is intended, and (for a participle-shaped modifier) the result of the definiteness-agreement test and the label it yields.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner uses an active participle to narrate a specific, bounded past event instead of the perfect verb the event actually requires.
A learner labels a definite, case-agreeing participle modifier a circumstantial (hal) without running the definiteness-agreement test that would identify it as an ordinary attribute instead.

arabic_grammar_name: ta'sis al-mustalah al-nahwi 'ala ma'nahu al-'arabi al-asli, wa fahs wujud al-fi'l qabla tasmiyat al-musnad ilayhi (grounding grammatical terminology in its own Arabic sense, and checking for a verb before naming the logical subject)
plain_rule: An Arabic grammatical category is learned from its own Arabic definition and its own licensing environment, never by mapping it onto the nearest English grammatical category, because several Arabic categories have no true English counterpart and the mapping distorts their actual licensing conditions (an English label imported wholesale can silently import English agreement or case rules that do not hold for the Arabic category). A memorized label is not an opaque code: decomposing it into its own ordinary Arabic components (a 'doer noun', an 'instrument noun') recovers the category's function directly, faster than a separate lookup table, whenever the label itself is forgotten. And when a sentence's logical subject is being named, the presence or absence of a verb is checked FIRST: a fa'il (agent) is licensed only where a verb is present and behaves by the verb's own agreement rules, while a mubtada' (topic) is licensed only in a verbless nominal sentence and behaves by different agreement rules with its predicate -- one English label ('the subject') must never cover both, since they have different licensers and different downstream behavior.
trigger_condition: an Arabic grammatical category's meaning or agreement behavior is being explained by mapping it onto an English category, a memorized label's function cannot be recalled, or a sentence's logical subject is being named without first checking for the presence of a verb
expected_feature: a category explained from its own Arabic definition and licensing environment rather than an English equivalent, a forgotten label's function recovered by decomposing it into its own ordinary components, and the presence or absence of a verb checked before choosing between fa'il and mubtada' (or any other verb-conditioned category pair)
typical_error_feature: an Arabic category's behavior explained by importing an English category's agreement or case rules; a memorized label treated as an opaque code with its function looked up rather than decomposed; or one English label ('the subject') applied to both a verb-licensed fa'il and a verbless-sentence mubtada' without checking which licensing environment is actually present
point_template: Before you explain this category, ground it in its own Arabic definition, not an English equivalent -- and before you name the logical subject, check whether a verb is actually present.
teach_template: An Arabic grammatical category is learned from its own Arabic definition and licensing environment, since mapping it onto an English category can silently import rules that do not hold; a forgotten label's function is recovered by decomposing it into its own ordinary Arabic components, not by rote lookup; and a fa'il (verb-licensed) and a mubtada' (verbless-sentence-licensed) are different categories with different downstream agreement behavior, so the presence or absence of a verb must be checked before either label is used.
bottom_out_template: State the category's own Arabic definition and licensing environment (not an English equivalent), and, for a subject-naming decision, whether a verb is present and which category that licenses.

curriculum_error_examples.en: A learner explains an Arabic grammatical category's behavior by mapping it onto the nearest English category, importing agreement or case rules that do not actually hold for it.
A learner uses one English label ('the subject') for both a verb-licensed agent and a verbless-sentence topic without first checking whether a verb is present.
